claim: Excessive Notch signalling in Drosophila neural stem cell (NSC) lineages results in supernumerary NSCs causing hyperplasia.
source: In Drosophila neural stem cell (NSC) lineages, excessive Notch signalling results in supernumerary NSCs causing hyperplasia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known phenomenon that forms the basis for the study.

claim: The onset of hyperplasia from excessive Notch signaling is considerably delayed.
source: However, onset of hyperplasia is considerably delayed implying there are mechanisms that resist the mitogenic signal.
evidence: This observation is stated in the abstract and is a key finding that motivates the study.

claim: Normal attenuation of E(spl)mγ is still initiated in NSC progeny in the presence of excess Notch activity.
source: Monitoring the live expression of a Notch target gene, E(spl)mγ, revealed that normal attenuation is still initiated in the presence of excess Notch activity so that re-emergence of NSC properties occurs only in older progeny.
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging experiments described in the abstract and results.

claim: Re-emergence of NSC properties occurs only in older progeny when excess Notch activity is present.
source: Monitoring the live expression of a Notch target gene, E(spl)mγ, revealed that normal attenuation is still initiated in the presence of excess Notch activity so that re-emergence of NSC properties occurs only in older progeny.
evidence: This is a key finding from live imaging experiments showing temporal dynamics of NSC marker expression.

claim: Depletion of Mi-2/NuRD ATP remodeling complex dramatically enhanced Notch-induced hyperplasia.
source: Screening for factors responsible, we found that depletion of Mi-2/NuRD ATP remodeling complex dramatically enhanced Notch-induced hyperplasia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNAi screen described in the abstract and results section.

claim: E(spl)mγ was no longer extinguished in NSC progeny when Mi-2 was depleted under conditions of excess Notch activity.
source: Under these conditions, E(spl)mγ was no longer extinguished in NSC progeny.
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging experiments with Mi-2 depletion.

claim: Mi-2 is required for decommissioning stem-cell enhancers in NSC progeny.
source: We propose that Mi-2 is required for decommissioning stem-cell enhancers in their progeny, enabling the switch towards more differentiated fates and rendering them insensitive to mitogenic factors such as Notch.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic proposal of the paper based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: A subset of cells in many solid tumours have characteristics of stem cells.
source: For example, a subset of the cells in many solid tumours (e.g glioblastomas, neuroblastomas) have characteristics of stem cells, deploying programmes that normal stem cells would use for tissue development and repair to support the development and progressive growth of the tumour (Azzarelli et al., 2018; Lathia et al., 2015; Reya et al., 2001; Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Drosophila neuroblasts divide asymmetrically to generate a larger daughter cell that retains stem-cell identity and a smaller daughter cell that follows a more differentiated fate.
source: Similar to mammalian neural stem cells, NBs divide asymmetrically to generate a larger daughter cell that retains stem-cell identity and a smaller daughter cell that will follow a more differentiated fate (Homem et al., 2015; Knoblich, 2008; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neuroblast biology supported by citations.

claim: Neuroblasts resume divisions in larval stages upon receiving nutrition signals from adjacent glial cells.
source: After entering quiescence at the end of embryogenesis, NBs resume divisions in larval stages, upon receiving proper nutrition signals from their adjacent glial cells (Chell and Brand, 2010; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Key cell fate determinants such as Prospero, Numb and Brat are segregated into the smaller progeny cell during neuroblast division.
source: In each division, key cell fate determinants such as Prospero, Numb and Brat are segregated into the smaller progeny cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about asymmetric cell division in neuroblasts.

claim: Loss of Numb or mechanisms giving excess Notch signalling can lead to hyperplasia.
source: For example, Numb inhibits Notch activity, and the loss of Numb or other mechanisms giving excess Notch signalling can lead to hyperplasia (Bowman et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2006a; Wang et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Type I lineages appear resistant to ectopic Notch activity as the majority of their daughter cells continue to be routed towards differentiation.
source: However, certain lineages, so-called Type I lineages, appear resistant to the ectopic Notch activity as the majority of their daughter cells continue to be routed towards differentiation even in these conditions.
evidence: This is an observation that forms a key motivation for the study.

claim: In Type I lineages, the smaller daughter Ganglion Mother Cell (GMC) divides only once to generate two post-mitotic neurons or glia cells.
source: In Type I lineages, the smaller daughter, so-called Ganglion Mother Cell (GMC), divides only once to generate two post-mitotic neurons or glia cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Type I neuroblast lineages.

claim: In Type II lineages, the smaller progeny become intermediate neural progenitors (INP) which divide three to six times asymmetrically.
source: In Type II lineages, the smaller progeny of the NBs become intermediate neural progenitors (INP), which then divide three to six times asymmetrically to self-renew and to generate GMCs that, like the GMCs derived from Type I NBs, then divide into two post-mitotic neurons or glia cells (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008; Izergina et al., 2009; Kang and Reichert, 2015; Knoblich, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Type II neuroblast lineages supported by citations.

claim: Both Type I and Type II neuroblasts exhibit high levels of Notch activity and express key targets deadpan (dpn), Enhancer of split-HLHmγ (E(spl)mγ) and klumpfuss (klu).
source: Both Type I and Type II neuroblasts exhibit high levels of Notch activity and express key targets deadpan (dpn), Enhancer of split-HLHmγ (E(spl)mγ) and klumpfuss (klu), that are shut off in the progeny (Almeida and Bray, 2005; Berger et al., 2012; San-Juán and Baonza, 2011; Xiao et al., 2012; Zacharioudaki et al., 2016; Zacharioudaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Type II lineages are highly sensitive to excessive Notch activity, which brings about ectopic expression of stem cell markers in INPs to drive NB-like behaviour and tumour formation.
source: Type II lineages are highly sensitive to excessive Notch activity, which brings about ectopic expression of stem cell markers in INPs to drive NB-like behaviour and tumour formation (Bowman et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2010; Zacharioudaki et al., 2016; Zacharioudaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Type I lineages only become hyperplastic under extreme conditions.
source: In contrast, Type I lineages only become hyperplastic under extreme conditions.
evidence: This is an observation that distinguishes Type I from Type II lineages.

claim: After 8 hr of exposure to active Notch, only 22% of Type I lineages turned hyperplastic.
source: In the early stages of Notch-driven hyperplasia (8 hr), only a small proportion of Type I lineages turned hyperplastic (22%, Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: E(spl)mγ and dpn were the first stem-cell markers to be expressed in hyperplastic Type I lineages.
source: Testing a panel of such stem-cell markers revealed that E(spl)mγ and dpn were the first to be expressed and, of the two, E(spl)mγ appeared to be the earliest as there was a subset of cells in hyperplastic lineages that express E(spl)mγ-GFP only (2 ± 0.2; Figure 1A,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of marker expression shown in Figure 1.

claim: After 24 hr of Nact expression, 36.3% of Type I lineages exhibited ectopic NB markers.
source: Continued expression of Nact for 24 hr led to an increase in the number of Type I lineages with ectopic NB markers (36.3%; Figure 1A,C)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: After 48 hr of Notch activity, 89.3% of Type I lineages became hyperplastic.
source: However, it was only with more prolonged Notch activity (48 hr) that the majority of lineages became hyperplastic (89.3%; Figure 1A,C)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells that acquired stem-cell characteristics were intermediate in size between a GMC and a NB.
source: Notably, the cells that acquired stem-cell characteristics were intermediate in size between a GMC and a NB, suggesting that they do not arise from a symmetrical division of a pre-existing NB.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data that informs the mechanism.

claim: NBs continued to divide asymmetrically even in the presence of excessive Notch signaling.
source: Furthermore, the NBs themselves continued to divide asymmetrically even in the presence of excessive Notch signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The extent of hyperplasia correlated with the duration of exposure to Notch activity, not the developmental stage at which NBs were exposed.
source: This yielded identical results, that is the extent of hyperplasia correlated with the duration of exposure not the developmental stage at which the NBs were exposed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experiments varying the timing of Notch exposure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In normal NBs, E(spl)mγ-GFP expression was rapidly extinguished in the GMC progeny.
source: In these conditions, normal NBs underwent asymmetric cell divisions and E(spl)mγ-GFP expression was rapidly extinguished in the GMC progeny (Figure 2A,C,E and Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: E(spl)mγ-GFP levels in NBs fluctuated with a defined temporal pattern through the cell cycle, with highest expression as NBs entered and exited mitosis.
source: In the NB itself the levels fluctuated, with a defined temporal pattern through the cell cycle where the highest expression occurred as the NBs entered and exited mitosis (Figure 2A,C,E and Figure 2—video 1.
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the presence of high levels of Notch activity, NBs continued to undergo asymmetric cell divisions and E(spl)mγ-GFP was extinguished in the GMC, albeit with slightly slower kinetics than in normal conditions.
source: In the presence of high levels of Notch activity, the NBs continued to undergo asymmetric cell divisions and the expression of E(spl)mγ-GFP was extinguished in the GMC, albeit with slightly slower kinetics than in normal conditions (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some NB progeny reacquired E(spl)mγ-GFP expression after a few hours in the presence of Nact.
source: After a few hours, however, some of the NB progeny reacquired E(spl)mγ-GFP expression.
evidence: This is a key observation from live imaging experiments.

claim: The reappearance of E(spl)mγ-GFP only occurred in progeny born before the onset of imaging (>8 hr earlier).
source: The reappearance of E(spl)mγ-GFP only occurred in progeny born before the onset of imaging (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—video 2), indicating that it must occur in cells that had been born from the NSC > 8 hr earlier.
evidence: This is based on tracking cells over time in live imaging experiments.

claim: Mi-2 depletion significantly enhanced the number of Dpn-positive cells elicited by Nact by 2.7-fold.
source: This significantly enhanced the number of Dpn-positive (Dpn+ve) cells elicited by Nact: the total number of Dpn expressing cells was enhanced 2.7-fold when Mi-2 was depleted compared to Nact alone (1322 ± 71 vs 485 ± 27; Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNAi screen shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mi-2 depletion alone was not sufficient to bring about any increase in Dpn+ve cells.
source: In contrast, Mi-2 depletion alone was not sufficient to bring about any increase in Dpn+ve cells (161 ± 2 vs 158 ± 2), despite that this treatment robustly extinguished Mi-2 protein levels in the NB lineages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a control experiment showing Mi-2 depletion alone has no effect.

claim: Knock down of MTA-like produced a 1.4-fold enhancement of Notch-induced hyperplasia.
source: Knock down of MTA-like (Figure 3B) or Caf1-p55 (Figure 3C) both produced a 1.4-fold enhancement of Notch-induced hyperplasia (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing other NuRD complex members shown in Figure 3.

claim: Knock down of Caf1-p55 produced a 1.4-fold enhancement of Notch-induced hyperplasia.
source: Knock down of MTA-like (Figure 3B) or Caf1-p55 (Figure 3C) both produced a 1.4-fold enhancement of Notch-induced hyperplasia (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing other NuRD complex members shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mi-2 functions in attenuating Notch activity via its participation in the NuRD complex.
source: Nevertheless, the results suggest that Mi-2 functions in attenuating Notch activity via its participation in the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of depleting multiple NuRD complex members.

claim: Depletion of Mi-2 alone had no discernible effect on E(spl)mγ-GFP in GMCs.
source: Depletion of Mi-2 alone had no discernible effect on E(spl)mγ-GFP in GMCs: it was extinguished as in normal conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in live imaging experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the context of Nact, Mi-2 depletion resulted in striking persistence of E(spl)mγ-GFP in GMCs in 27.8% of lineages.
source: However, in the context of Nact there was a striking persistence of E(spl)mγ-GFP in the GMCs in a substantial proportion of lineages (27.8%; Figure 4A–E and Figure 4—video 2,3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from live imaging shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mi-2/NuRD complex has an important role in suppressing the ability of stem-cell progeny to respond to Notch.
source: These data demonstrate therefore that Mi-2/NuRD complex has an important role in suppressing the ability of the stem-cell progeny to respond to Notch and suggests that it contributes to the shut-down of stem-cell promoting genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the live imaging experiments showing persistence of E(spl)mγ-GFP.

claim: Down-regulating Mi-2 by RNAi resulted in a robust increase in the expression of E(spl)mβ and E(spl)m3 in Kc cells.
source: Down-regulating Mi-2 by treating cells with RNAi resulted in a robust increase in the expression of E(spl)mβ, Ε(spl)m3 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a result from qPCR experiments in cultured cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: The effects of Mi-2 depletion on E(spl) gene expression were similar to those seen when Hairless was depleted.
source: These effects were similar to those seen when the co-repressor Hairless was depleted (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a comparison of effects from depleting different factors shown in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of Mi-2 in the context of Notch signalling activation led to enhanced induction of E(spl) genes.
source: Furthermore, loss of Mi-2 in the context of conditions where Notch signalling was activated, led to an enhanced induction of the E(spl) genes that are normally up-regulated in these conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in experiments with Notch activation in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of Mi-2 leads to de-repression of E(spl) genes and other Notch regulated genes in Notch off conditions.
source: Thus, loss of Mi-2 leads to de-repression of E(spl) genes and of other Kc cell Notch targets in Notch off conditions and enhances their activation in Notch on conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the effects observed in Kc cell experiments.

claim: Concomitant knock down of both Mi-2 and Hairless led to much greater de-repression of E(spl)mβ and E(spl)m3 than from either knock down alone.
source: In contrast, concomitant knock down of both Mi-2 and Hairless led to a much greater de-repression of E(spl)mβ and E(spl)m3 than from either knock down alone, suggesting the two factors work independently to repress these genes (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in double knockdown experiments in Figure 5.

claim: No interaction between Su(H) and Mi-2 was detected.
source: In agreement, no interaction between Su(H) and Mi-2 was detected (Figure 5F) arguing that Mi-2 acts independently of the SuH-Hairless co-repressor complex to attenuate the expression of E(spl) genes.
evidence: This is shown in co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5F.

claim: Loss of Mi-2 had no effect on Su(H) recruitment in either Notch off or Notch on conditions.
source: However, loss of Mi-2 had no effect on Su(H) recruitment in either Notch off or Notch on conditions (Figure 5G)
evidence: This is shown in ChIP experiments in Figure 5G.

claim: Loss of Mi-2 did not affect the levels of H3K27 trimethylation or H3K27ac at Notch target enhancers.
source: neither did it affect the levels of H3K27 trimethylation, the repressive histone modification deposited by Polycomb complexes, or of H3K27ac (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is shown in ChIP experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 72% of Su(H) bound regions overlapped with Mi-2 occupied sites in Kc cells.
source: Strikingly, 72% of Su(H) bound regions overlapped with Mi-2 occupied sites.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome-wide ChIP data.

claim: Mi-2 is present at significant levels at the E(spl)mβ and E(spl)m3 regulatory regions.
source: These included significant enrichments for Mi-2 at the E(spl)mβ and E(spl)m3 regulatory regions in the E(spl)-C (Figure 5A), which we verified by ChIP qPCR (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown in ChIP-qPCR experiments in Figure 5H.

claim: Mi-2 binds directly to Notch target genes and exerts a repressive effect on them independently of Su(H) and Hairless.
source: In summary, Mi-2 binds directly to Notch target genes and exerts a repressive effect on them, even in Kc cells, but it appears to do so independently of Su(H) and Hairless.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the Kc cell experiments.

claim: Depletion of Zfh1 significantly enhanced Nact-induced hyperplasia.
source: Of those tested, only two factors significantly enhanced the hyperplasia, namely Prospero and Zfh1, indicating that they were plausible candidates to recruit Mi-2 (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in experiments testing candidate factors in Figure 6.

claim: Depletion of Prospero significantly enhanced Nact-induced hyperplasia.
source: Of those tested, only two factors significantly enhanced the hyperplasia, namely Prospero and Zfh1, indicating that they were plausible candidates to recruit Mi-2 (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in experiments testing candidate factors in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of Zfh1 was sufficient to significantly reduce the number of Dpn+ve cells.
source: Indeed, expression of either Prospero or Zfh1 was sufficient to significantly reduce the number of Dpn+ve cells, suggesting they have suppressed NB identity (Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in overexpression experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Depletion of Mi-2 partially overcame the effects of Zfh1 overexpression, restoring the number of NBs to close to normal levels.
source: Furthermore, depletion of Mi-2 partially overcame the effects of Zfh1 overexpression, restoring the number of NBs to close to normal levels (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is shown in epistasis experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Mi-2 depletion failed to rescue the effects from Prospero over-expression.
source: In contrast, Mi-2 depletion failed to rescue the effects from Prospero over-expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in epistasis experiments in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zfh1 overexpression attenuated Notch-induced hyperplasia, an effect that was partially abolished by loss of Mi-2.
source: In agreement, Zfh1 overexpression attenuated the Notch-induced hyperplasia, an effect that was partially abolished by loss of Mi-2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B)
evidence: This is shown in experiments combining Zfh1 overexpression with Mi-2 depletion in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Zfh1 cooperates with Mi-2 to suppress stem-cell identity.
source: Together these data argue that Zfh1 cooperates with Mi-2 to suppress stem-cell identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Zfh1 was detected in the progeny located in proximity to the NB and in Asense-labelled GMCs in Type I NB lineages.
source: Indeed, using a fly line in which the endogenous Zfh1 is fused to GFP (Albert et al., 2018). Zfh1 was detected in the progeny that are located in proximity to the NB and in the Asense-labelled GMCs, albeit at lower levels (Figure 6E) in Type I NB lineages.
evidence: This is shown using a Zfh1-GFP reporter in Figure 6E.

claim: Zfh1 was absent from the NB and INPs in Type II lineages.
source: In contrast, Zfh1 was absent from the NB and INPs in Type II lineages albeit these cells exhibited strong or moderate Mi-2 levels, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Zfh1 is an important intermediary in recruiting Mi-2/NuRD complex to shut off stem-cell enhancers in the NB progeny of Type I lineages.
source: Together the results point to Zfh1 as an important intermediary in recruiting Mi-2/NuRD complex to shut off stem-cell enhancers in the NB progeny of Type I lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression pattern and genetic interaction data.

claim: Mi-2/NuRD complex functions to decommission stem-cell enhancers in differentiating progeny, rendering them resistant to stem-cell promoting factors like Notch.
source: Thus, we propose that Mi-2/NuRD complex functions to decommission the stem-cell enhancers in the differentiating progeny (Figure 7) rendering them resistant to stem-cell promoting factors like Notch (Whyte et al., 2012).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic model proposed based on all the data.

claim: NuRD will be widely deployed in developmental transitions to decommission enhancers in readiness for subsequent lineage decisions.
source: As the iterative use of signaling pathways, including Notch, is important throughout development to generate different tissue and cell types, it is likely that NuRD will be widely deployed in such developmental transitions to decommission enhancers in readiness for subsequent lineage decisions.
evidence: This is a speculation about broader implications of the findings.

claim: NuRD is found at most sites of active transcription in embryonic stem cells.
source: Although originally considered a repressive complex, NuRD is found at most sites of active transcription in embryonic stem cells, where it appears to fine-tune gene expression as well as having a major role in allowing cells to exit self-renewal (Bornelöv et al., 2018; de Dieuleveult et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2016; Reynolds et al., 2012a; Reynolds et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mammalian homologue ZEB2 cooperates with NuRD complex to antagonise Notch in Schwann cells.
source: This is similar to the role proposed for the mammalian homologue ZEB2 during Schwann Cell differentiation, where it engages the NuRD complex to antagonise Notch and Sox2 (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A missense mutation in Zeb2 that abolished its association with the NuRD complex rendered it incapable of promoting Schwann Cell differentiation.
source: Indeed, a missense mutation in the Zeb2 that abolished its association with the NuRD complex rendered it incapable of promoting Schwann Cell differentiation (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Eyeless/Pax6 is switched on in the progeny of old Type II NBs and makes them refractory to Notch.
source: For example eyeless/Pax6 is switched on in the progeny of old Type II NBs and makes them refractory to Notch (Farnsworth et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ikaros expression during T-cell differentiation shapes the timing and repertoire of Notch target genes.
source: and Ikaros expression during T-cell differentiation shapes the timing and repertoire of Notch target genes (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ikaros was found to associate with the Mi-2/NuRD complex.
source: Whether these factors rely on Mi-2 remains to be explored but as Ikaros was found to associate with the Mi-2/NuRD complex, it could rely on similar mechanism to Zfh1/Zeb2 (Sridharan and Smale, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PROX1, the mammalian homologue of Prospero, interacted with NuRD complex to suppress Notch pathway in colorectal cancer cells.
source: Likewise, PROX 1, the mammalian homologue of Prospero, interacted with NuRD complex to suppress Notch pathway in colorectal cancer cells.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge without a specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Type II neuroblast lineages are exquisitely sensitive to ectopic Notch activity because they lack factor(s) that recruit Mi-2 to target enhancers.
source: Conversely, the fact that Type II neuroblast lineages are exquisitely sensitive to ectopic Notch activity argues that these cells lack factor(s) that recruit Mi-2 to the target enhancers.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity of Type I vs Type II lineages.

claim: An alternate mechanism involving the repressor earmuff/dFezf is deployed to repress the competence of INPs to respond to Notch targets in Type II lineages.
source: Indeed Zfh1 is not expressed in the intermediate progeny of these lineages and it has been shown that an alternate mechanism, involving the repressor earmuff/dFezf is deployed to repress the competence of INPs to respond to Notch targets and thus their dedifferentiation into NBs (Janssens et al., 2014; Koe et al., 2014). .
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prolonged Notch activity can ultimately reprogramme progeny towards stem-cell fates, driving hyperplasia even in the presence of Mi2.
source: The fact that prolonged Notch activity can ultimately reprogramme progeny towards the stem-cell fates, driving hyperplasia even in the presence of Mi2, argues that NuRD is not fully silencing target genes.
evidence: This is based on the observation that hyperplasia eventually occurs even with Mi-2 present.

claim: NuRD is involved in fine-tuning transcriptional responses.
source: This fits with the model that NuRD is involved in fine-tuning transcriptional responses (Bornelöv et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.
